utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers, if you could finish as soon as possible, to give Mr. Kovacic his chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've arranged an equitable distribution, Mr. President. I will try to be through between 10.30 and quarter to 11, and I believe Mr. Kovacic anticipates having approximately one hour of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break rather before then, at 10.15 or so, to 10.20, and you should aim to be through by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will try to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, we left yesterday discussing the incident in which Commander Zivko Totic was kidnapped in Zenica. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You felt, yourself, that with that kidnapping, events were starting to run away from you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a way of phrasing it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you and your commanding officer ever discuss the multiple murder, and kidnapping of the HVO commander in Zenica, as a potential spark that could cause the entire Lasva Valley to erupt in fighting?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss it. We certainly said that it was not going to do anything to help the situation. I don't remember saying anything about the whole Lasva Valley going up in flames, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stewart ever express the view to you, as far as you can recall, Colonel Watters, that this kidnapping incident created a terribly volatile atmosphere that could potentially be the catalyst for the eruption of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed the fact that it was certainly prejudicial to the current alliance between the two factions. I remember discussing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to show you a milinfosum, number 94.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D61/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And specifically the entry on this milinfosum dated February the 2nd, 1993, that I would like to draw your attention to, appears on page 2, note 4. Was it your understanding that the 333rd Highland Brigade of the BiH army had its headquarters in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just look at this note 4, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I've read note 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that the 333rd Highland Brigade of the BH army had its headquarters located in the village of Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It certainly was BritBat's view on the 2nd of February, according to this milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any disagreement with that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that elements of the 7th Muslim Brigade had been deployed north of Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I give you the same answer to that: That's what it says in the milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, was the BritBat contingent ever able to develop any reliable information about the 7th Muslim Brigade at any time during your tour of duty in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had a wide variety of sources of information on that and many other units. As to the reliability of that information, I should think that was always subject to question, because it largely depended on the source from which we gained the information, and we would evaluate the relevant merit of that information. I would probably be sticking my neck out to say that our judgement on these situations was particularly reliable. It was the best we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me turn your attention now to the situation that confronted you on April the 15th, in the -- at night. As I understand it, Colonel Stewart was in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Leaving you as the commanding officer of the BritBat contingent in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that's a technical point. He still was the commanding officer, but communications were so difficult that if he was unable to be contacted on the radio or for periods of time, as his deputy, I would automatically assume command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. As I understand it, in the early morning of April the 16th, you began to receive reports from the Dutch battalion, based in Santici, of hostilities that had broken out?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Dutch battalion camp in Santici was located right next door to Ahmici, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, right across the main supply route?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact, the Dutch battalion camp overlooked the village of Ahmici, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Overlooked" would indicate it was on higher ground. It was actually on level or slightly lower ground, so it looked across and slightly up towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you actually did see Colonel Blaskic on April the 16th of 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, I did. I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you met him at his headquarters in Vitez, I believe, he looked to you completely calm and rational, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, he looked like he was in control and at war?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that the commander of the Muslim forces in Vitez was Sefkija Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And although hard pressed, he put up a successful defence of Stari Vitez, did he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true that notwithstanding what was, in your view, a surprise attack on the morning of April the 16th against the Muslim forces in Stari Vitez, the Muslim forces nonetheless conducted a successful defence of their positions?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that they continued to defend their positions in Stari Vitez for the ensuing ten months?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that you dispatched patrols in Warrior armoured patrol carriers -- or armoured personnel carriers; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Armoured fighting vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Armoured fighting vehicles, up and down the length of the Lasva Valley on April the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in the ensuing days as well?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it's true that these vehicles drove along the main road past both the villages of Santici and Ahmici; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that your patrols found dead bodies in Croat villages too, albeit not on the same scale as in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That would be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The same is true in Vitez as well, Croat bodies were found, I think five dead bodies; not on the scale of the Muslim dead, but nonetheless dead on both sides?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your view, I think you've said this, this was a military operation conducted by the Croats on a regional military level; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: By Colonel Blaskic, who was the regional HVO military commander?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, I believe you've already identified two headquarters of the BiH army, one located in the town of Vitez itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And one located in the village of Kruscica, approximately one kilometre to the south of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that there were other --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was actually a little further than one kilometre south, but it was to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How far was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: A couple of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two kilometres. All right. Would it be fair to say that you did not know that the BiH also had headquarters for their forces in the villages of Preocica and Poculica, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't visit those headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But did you know that the BiH army actually had forces and headquarters located in those two villages?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I suspect we probably did. I don't recollect the detail of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, looking at the forces on both sides on April the 16th, Colonel Watters, would it be fair to say that BritBat was aware that the BiH army consisted of seven separate corps, including the 3rd Corps headquartered in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many soldiers are there in a corps?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that General Hadzihasanovic estimated that the forces available to the BiH army numbered approximately 52.000?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised, but that would probably be in the entire Central Bosnian region or the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to take a look at milinfosum number 112, dated February the 19th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D62/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I need not detain you very long with this milinfosum, Colonel Watters. I would just like to address your attention to item number 3. Approximately halfway down, it says: "The 3rd Corps commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic, was also present at the school. He stated casually, in a conversation with the LO, that the Jajce Brigade formed part of the 52.000 BiH soldiers in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That will therefore have been what we put down. That's what the 3rd Corps commander said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that accurate, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand, but were you aware of any information that led you to conclude that that estimate of manpower was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean sitting here six years on, I can't remember what corroboration we had. I mean we would have listened to what the 3rd Corps commander said and recorded it in our milinfosum. If that was the size of the sort of BiH in Central Bosnia, it wouldn't have surprised us, I suspect. As it says there, "a fair assessment of the strength," that's the comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Were you of the view that the HVO had approximately 12.000 troops at their disposal in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That figure does ring a bell, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would concede, therefore, that the troops available to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina outnumbered the HVO troops by a considerable margin?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that, but that is not how we assessed or would assess, as professional soldiers, the combat power of the two relevant armies. Manpower is only one factor, and it's a rather spurious factor to look at the relevant combat power of two forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You actually saw BiH tanks in the area of operations for which you were responsible?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I saw two T-55s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never saw any HVO tanks, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in Prozor. I also saw tanks in Maglaj of a joint BiH-HVO brigade that had been captured from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was to the north of your area of operations, I believe, the northernmost part.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any tanks in Central Bosnia along the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree that Vitez is certainly within mortar range of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And vice versa. Colonel Watters, did you have a soldier under your command by the name of Corporal Gough (phoen), Vincent Gough?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had 612 soldiers. His name doesn't actually leap to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Are you familiar with the concept of FIBUA or "Fighting In Built-Up Areas"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that a standard tactical doctrine in the British army?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The term is now slightly outdated, but it is a doctrine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it a standard tactical doctrine in 1993 in the British army?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I would just like to ask you a few questions in connection with this doctrine, if I may. In the absence of earthen fortifications, it would be completely normal, in military operations, to use any available structure for defensive purposes, would it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In areas where fighting has occurred and a village has been taken and retained by an opposing force, that village is likely to be extremely heavily damaged at the end of the hostilities, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Stalingrad was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's common in the FIBUA doctrine for a platoon commander to give orders to his sections or manoeuvre units to secure a building or set of buildings, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The decisions on how to do that are actually made by the section commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't follow that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Decisions on how to effectuate the particular tactical objective are made by the section commander?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The section commander would be given an area of responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The section commander would decide which soldiers would lay down the initial field of fire; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And which ones would throw grenades into a house; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, which soldiers entered the house would be the decision of the section commander?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the FIBUA doctrine that the British army was trained to use in 1993, one of the overriding principles was the use of all available fire-power to clear houses; was that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Both direct and indirect fire; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mortars and machine gun fire?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The houses on either side of a particular target would be neutralised with supporting fire as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, you taught your soldiers, under the FIBUA doctrine, not to enter, if they could possibly avoid it, through doors or windows, but rather to blow a hole in the side of the house with a satchel charge or a tank shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know where the tank shell came from, but correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then after this hole had been blown in the side of the house, under the doctrine --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I see, you mean a tank to fire at the side of a house?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't subscribe to that personally, but you would try and enter the house by other means than the normal doors and windows, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Because of the danger of being shot at through those --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Then the doctrine teaches that grenades should be thrown in through any available opening, be it a hole blown in the side of the house or a door or a window; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To neutralise any soldiers that might be in the house, shooting at you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then the troops would charge in, shooting into the room; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They would also charge in, shooting through the ceiling --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and through the floor?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That is to avoid being shot themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Colonel Watters, that you had not actually been to the village of Ahmici yourself before April the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Driving along the main road, could you actually see, on April the 16th, the fact that the minaret had been toppled?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I could show you or ask you to look at Z1593,A, one of the Prosecution's set of exhibits, 1593,A. If the usher could put photograph number 22 on the ELMO, that might be helpful. Colonel Watters, we've seen the photos that you took from your Warrior armoured fighting vehicle, and the minaret actually did not have any graffiti on it. The photograph that I've just shown you has graffiti on it. Do you have any idea who put that graffiti on there or when?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, and I don't know what it means either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't see any graffiti at any time on the minaret during your tour of duty through the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in your opinion, Colonel Blaskic was in full command of all HVO troops before Ahmici, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In your opinion, Colonel Blaskic was in full command of all HVO troops during Ahmici, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was -- it's a slightly ambiguous question. I've already stated that there were occasions when soldiers appeared to disobey the orders of Colonel Blaskic. Colonel Blaskic was the regional military commander and therefore was in command of all HVO troops in the region, but as our experience showed, there were troops that did not follow the orders of Colonel Blaskic. I've made that point yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In your opinion, Colonel Blaskic was in full command of all HVO troops after Ahmici too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the same way as he was before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Watters, let me just address your attention to your testimony in the Blaskic case where you were asked those three questions by the Prosecutor. Page 3454 and 3455. Let me just read the questions and the answer. Mr. Kehoe said:

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry. Colonel Blaskic was in command of the HVO troops before Ahmici, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And after Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was the testimony that you gave; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, and that's what I've just affirmed. Colonel Blaskic was the regional military commander in command of all troops. I was asked the question yesterday were there any troops that didn't always follow his orders, and I said, yes, there were. He was still in command of the central military district that we operated in, but as was illustrated yesterday, there were incidents where troops did not follow his orders. But he was in command. That was the question I was asked. He was the regional commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that your information about the reasons that you ultimately concluded that Ahmici had been attacked came from Muslim sources?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The initial report we received, as you said yourself, was from the Dutch transport base, that Ahmici was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the esoteric and psychic reasons for the attack that you testified about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true that the sources for your conclusions regarding the esoteric and psychic reasons for the attack were exclusively from the Muslim side; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During your personal observation of the Ahmici battleground, you never saw any evidence of any mortar or artillery fire, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you described yesterday a conversation with Colonel Blaskic in which he had claimed that first, it may have been the Serb forces that attacked Ahmici; and second, that it could have been the Muslim forces themselves, that attacked themselves so to speak, and you found that patently ludicrous. Do you remember that today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you don't know whether Colonel Blaskic was aware of what had actually gone on at Ahmici when you had that conversation with him, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: My belief at that time was he was fully aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you don't know that for a fact, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall the quotation from Colonel Stewart's book that I read to you yesterday regarding conversations with Colonel Colm Doyle?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If a person had not been aware of what had gone on in Ahmici, given that state of affairs in Central Bosnia, is it your opinion that it would have been unreasonable for Colonel Blaskic to have entertained that view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that these are matters, really, for the witness. These are matters of argument. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the truck bomb that you testified about, I believe it exploded on April the 18th, 1993, in Stari Vitez, Colonel Watters; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that the bomb had actually exploded outside of the Muslim forces' military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was certainly in the region of that, yes. Outside the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you also testified that the Muslims, Muslim forces in Stari Vitez, were holding their own as of April the 17th, 18th, and 19th; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How were they doing that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: With defended infantry positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In other words, they were using weapons to fire back at the Croat attackers?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Using rifles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And they were doing so successfully?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the subject of the shelling of Zenica on April the 19th, 1993, about which you testified, would it be fair to say that it is extremely difficult, in your professional experience, with your 26 years of professional experience, to tell where artillery has been fired from?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The artillery shell and the mortar, in your professional experience, are not particularly accurate weapons, are they?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, they're area weapons, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's difficult to judge precisely where the projectiles will fall; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That would depend on the skill of the users, their experience, whether they fired ranging shots; it's too general a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any ranging shots were fired on Zenica on April the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point being, though, Colonel Watters, that artillery is basically an area weapon rather than a precision weapon; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this is especially true as the range increases?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At extreme ranges, the weapon is less and less precise?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. But there again, Zenica is a very big target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, on April the 19th, just to summarise, I believe that the Croats were faced with a very vigorous and successful Muslim counterattack?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: April 19th.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Croats found themselves forced into a dangerous defensive position; they were actually facing military defeat. Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At the best, a prolonged village-to-village firefight; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that would inevitably involve a substantial number of both military and civilian casualties; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. That was something that I discussed with General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that is when Zenica was shelled?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that most large cities and towns in Central Bosnia had been regularly shelled in the civil war at some time or another?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that Zenica had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But what's the answer to the question? Travnik, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Travnik was shelled, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Donji Vakuf, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Novi Travnik, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would hardly call it a city. It's a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was regularly shelled, though, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The whole of Bosnia was regularly shelled, and Sarajevo was regularly shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's what I was getting at. Now, the 3rd Corps actually had its headquarters in Zenica, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How do you know that the 3rd Corps headquarters was not the target?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because you -- I mean, that's a ridiculous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a minute, Colonel. There's a note here from the stenographers: "Kindly slow down for the purposes of the record." Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I stand, once again, justly accused and chastised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson points out that it is the pause which is important between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the question was, how do you know that the 3rd Corps headquarters was not the target?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that the 3rd -- the 3rd Corps headquarters wasn't the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think, as you put it in prior testimony in other cases, sir, this was a, quote, "Stop attacking us or we will flatten your city type of threat," unquote?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it worked, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes and no. I don't think, in the end, it was the actual decision that caused General Halilovic to decide not to press on and destroy Busovaca as a reprisal for the destruction of Ahmici. I think he actually evaluated other factors. Because he had already demonstrated, as had the BiH, that they were prepared to take civilian casualties in order to prosecute their military objectives. So again, I think it's a rather simplistic analysis to think that he actually succumbed to it. It was certainly a very visible threat to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You initially confronted Colonel Blaskic about the shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he suggested to you that it may have been Serb artillery?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact, you thought that there was actually a twisted logic to that suggestion, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a twisted logic to just about everything in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you would agree with me, sir, that you cannot be sure that it was actually Croat artillery that was used to shell Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time, with an artillery officer, we went to a great deal of trouble to try and ascertain whether it could be Serb artillery, and we couldn't -- unless the Serbs had managed to move artillery in front of their front lines, we couldn't see which Serb artillery could have fired it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you could never prove which artillery piece had actually fired the rounds, could you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there was only coincidental evidence that there was a weapon of -- a piece of Croat artillery of sufficient calibre, with sufficient range, that was firing at the same time, and that was documented. But that, again, is not proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that you would agree that Colonel Blaskic was the artillery commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those resources were part of his command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was in charge of the artillery?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Therefore the military action, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me turn to the ceasefire negotiations that you either mediated yourself or participated in. As I understand it, sir, the first negotiation occurred between the commander of the Muslim forces, Mr. Dzidic, and I believe that you said the commander of the forces in Vitez or Colonel Blaskic; you could not be sure which.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was there any signed ceasefire agreement that resulted from that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember whether a document was actually signed, but there was certainly an agreement to a ceasefire. That was at about lunchtime, 12.00 or so, on the morning of the 16th. I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've already testified, I believe, that Mr. Kordic took no part in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He wasn't invited?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: He wasn't -- he wasn't invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next event, chronologically, in the peace negotiation process, I understand, was the announcement of a peace document that had been signed by Mr. Mate Boban and President Izetbegovic on April the 18th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, as we said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Boban was a member of BiH parliament?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was he a member of the parliament? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was a -- as you said yesterday, he was the senior member of the HVO government in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I understand the next item chronologically, Colonel Blaskic issued a written ceasefire order on April the 18th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But that was not accepted by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then the next development occurred in Zenica, I believe, where high-level negotiations between senior authorised representatives of the hostile forces confronting one another --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- were present, and I believe General Morillon was there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Along with ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that resulted in a signed document, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to look at the document that has previously been marked as D24/1. Once again, Colonel Watters, this document need not detain us long. Is this a copy of the ceasefire agreement that was signed in Zenica on the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It certainly looks like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was never invited to attend these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't involved in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I understand it, the next item that occurred in these negotiations was another meeting at the BritBat base in Stari Bila, on April the 21st?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next day?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was attended by General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was the chief of staff of the HVO --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We did all this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I quite agree. We are going over material which isn't in dispute. Can we move on, please? If there's a general point that Mr. Kordic was not involved in the negotiations, that, of course, can be put. But that apart, I don't see there is much point going over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While Mr. Sayers is finding his place in his notes, I've noticed the long passage of cross-examination about fighting in built-up areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the significance of it might be explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might turn your attention to the next document I would like to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D63/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: While we look at this, Colonel Watters, it was suggested that we ask you whether you would agree that Mr. Kordic was not involved in any of the ceasefire or peace negotiations in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he wasn't directly, and as I said yesterday, the only time his name was mentioned was when I mentioned it to General Petkovic to be sure that he wasn't going to unravel what was being agreed and implemented by Colonel Blaskic, because in the past he had appeared not to comply with Colonel Blaskic's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to Exhibit D63/1, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the response was?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean, in general terms, yes. I mean, I can't -- I'm not party to any individual conversations that may have taken place between Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you the next document, which is dated April the 23rd, 1993, and is Colonel Blaskic's reply to Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D64/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, do you know whether a joint commission was ever formed consisting of representatives of the BiH army and HVO to investigate the events at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just reading this letter. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The question, I think, was, do you know whether a joint commission was ever formed consisting of representatives of the BiH army and HVO to investigate the events at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not during our time there. I don't remember it. I remember Colonel Stewart being exasperated, angered, and frustrated at the lack of preparedness of the HVO, and specifically Colonel Blaskic, to take any action against the people that we believed he knew had conducted this atrocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know why such a joint commission as the one suggested by Colonel Blaskic was not formed?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have a vague memory that the BiH didn't believe there was a point in forming a joint commission to investigate an atrocity conducted by the HVO. But again, I mean, the detail, I'm afraid, is long -- is long gone from my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, that's perfectly all right, but it's your recollection that the BiH representatives declined to participate in such a joint commission?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The point of the joint commission was a complete smokescreen to enable the HVO to avoid investigating their own soldiers for the murder of civilians. And the BiH declined to take part because they also saw it as a smokescreen. I am not defending the BiH; they were equally -- and did commit very similar murders, as we have discussed. Neither side were the good guys or the bad guys; they were both good and bad guys. It just depended who was doing what to whom at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me move on to another area. At some point, the representatives of the ECMM and the U.N. Centre for Human Rights arrived in your area of responsibility to perform an investigation themselves, did they not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who made the arrangements for these gentlemen to visit your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know when that was done?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were several visits to the area. There was certainly one conducted by United Nations investigators shortly after the incident. I can remember taking some of them around Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you personally brief those investigators?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, there were several visits; some Colonel Stewart briefed, some I briefed. I certainly briefed some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall who you briefed?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were two: a gentleman called Payam, and I can't remember the other gentleman's name. They were two Americans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does the name "Osorio" sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How long did you spend briefing these gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: They visited us for a couple of days. I spent time talking to them, and I spent a few hours with them in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that UNPROFOR and various other organisations actually compiled a list of suspects, those organisations believed to have been involved --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: We talked about this yesterday, yes. It produced a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And your testimony was, I believe, that Colonel Blaskic was given a list of 11 suspects?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, the number is to the best of my memory. He was certainly given the list by Colonel Stewart, as I remember. I wouldn't like the Court to believe, from my evidence, that that was the total number of people who took part. That was just a list of some of the people who took part, as we believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember giving this testimony in the Blaskic case two years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, the HVO was never given any information derived from the victims and survivors of Ahmici from which they could build and further their own investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, can you say that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. This is from page 3553 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, the HVO was never given any information derived from the victims and survivors of Ahmici from which they could build and further their own investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That would appear to be different to what I'm saying now. I would have to know the context of that question, what the previous questions were before and what I was actually being asked. For example, we did not receive information from the victims. We received information from other sources, and it was that information from other sources that we gave to -- as I remember it, Colonel Stewart gave to Colonel Blaskic. You would need to actually put that question and my answer in context. I certainly don't remember saying we did not confront the HVO with the facts as we knew them, as they developed, so I don't quite understand my answers to the question. It would need to be put in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, are you sure that this list of names was given to the HVO by Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Whether it was given or not, as I said yesterday, I can't remember. Colonel Stewart certainly had a list of names. He confronted Colonel Blaskic with that list of names. I think Colonel Stewart gave Colonel Blaskic the list of names. The source of the list of names was very sensitive, and I know that was an overriding factor on Colonel Stewart's judgement as to what he did with that list of names. You would have to ask Colonel Stewart the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me read you a passage from Colonel Stewart's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is Colonel Stewart going to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm certainly intending to call Colonel Stewart. He is a listed witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's pointless to go on in this way when we're going to have Colonel Stewart, who can deal with the matters himself. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, you are aware that Colonel Blaskic did endeavour to find out the names of those whom he believed to be responsible for events at Ahmici, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean I'm not aware what Colonel Blaskic got up to, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember giving this testimony at page 3456 of the Blaskic transcript two years ago?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am aware that Colonel Blaskic endeavoured to find out the names of those he believed responsible, and I understand that he passed those names up his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, can you read the whole context of my evidence? That sentence, on its own, a little like the ridiculous sentences you quoted yesterday from my letter to my father, when taken in isolation can mean something completely different, and I can't put in context something I said two years ago about something that happened six years ago with a single sentence, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me read to you the question and the answer, sir. Lines 17 through 23 of the transcript on November the 10th, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Colonel, were any such acts to investigate and prosecute the individuals involved in those atrocities done by the defendant?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am aware that Colonel Blaskic endeavoured to find out the names of those he believed responsible, and I understand that he passed those names up his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would only caveat if I said that two years ago, it's what I thought and believed when I said it. I would only caveat it to say that that is what Colonel Blaskic said he did, and if Colonel Blaskic said that, then I would have acknowledged that he had said it. I can't possibly say that I know he did it because I didn't know he did it, but I would certainly say he said he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to the last few subjects that I want to cover with you. First of all, your conversation with Dario Kordic, this occurred in the basement of a building in Busovaca, the town of Busovaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the bank, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. The purpose of that meeting, I believe, was to try to resolve issues of stolen vehicles.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember any details of the meeting other than I was going to be introduced to him, and I think the conversation either -- conducted by the liaison officer, through the interpreter, with me as a party to it did cover a range of subjects, and I think that was one of them. We were certainly grateful to Mr. Kordic for having arranged the release earlier of a soldier, this BritBat from Kiseljak, and his involvement in the returning of stolen vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that if you had problems that needed to be resolved in the immediate area of Busovaca, you would try to contact Mr. Kordic for help in that regard?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would never think of going to him to help out with those kinds of problems in the town of Vitez, for example, would you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Well, that's not actually true, because the Dutch vehicle was actually abducted from close to Vitez. It wasn't abducted in Busovaca, and he enabled the return of that vehicle due to, we presume, the control he exercised over those elements of the HVO that had taken that vehicle or had influenced themselves over the criminal elements that had taken that vehicle. So that's the context of it. It wasn't confined just to the environs of Busovaca, his influence, in our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Isn't it true that in your opinion and experience, Mr. Kordic's influence, if any, did not seem to stretch beyond Busovaca and its close environs?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have just answered that question. He appeared to exercise a degree of military control in Busovaca and its environs. His political control and influence seemed to stretch beyond that, in that he was able to return the Dutch vehicle that had been taken from outside Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember testifying in the Blaskic case two years ago that Mr. Kordic's authority, if any, "mostly applied to Busovaca and its close environs. It did not seem to stretch much beyond that, in terms of the particular problems that we had"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as I've just said, yes. And define "close environs". I mean I was interpreting that as the area around Busovaca that Busovaca influenced, which also included areas of Vitez, hence the return of the Dutch vehicle that Blaskic was unable to achieve but Kordic was able to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To your understanding, the local mafiosi were unhappy about the return of that vehicle, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday about some perceived cooling, I believe was the word that you used, in the relationship between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic after the HVO had been surrounded and pushed back on their heels; right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was a personal perception, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Did you ever speak to Mr. Kordic about that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Mr. Blaskic about that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What were your sources?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The exchange at the meeting between myself, General Petkovic, and Colonel Blaskic, when I had raised the issue of Mr. Kordic, and also reports of sort of the general conversation heard by our LOs through their interpreters during the period afterwards. It was just a perception, as I said. It was impossible to give a single piece of corroboration to. It was my perception. It might have been wrong. It was my perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to the testimony that you gave regarding the halted convoy, it would be fair to say that there is no reference to that incident in your September the 1st, 1994 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'd have to read it. I mean I'm sorry, I don't remember something I said in 1994. I was asked a series of questions and I gave a series of answers to those questions, and if I wasn't asked a question about Mr. Kordic, I probably wouldn't have given an answer about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure if there is a statement in there, that will be pointed out to you. Let me turn to the statement that you wrote on April the 17th, 1997, consisting of some 23 pages. There's no reference to the convoy incident in that statement either, is there, Colonel Watters?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: You ask that as if it's an accusation. I mean if you say there isn't, well, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there is any reference to --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't worry about the questions. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there is any reference to that incident in any milinfosum, Colonel Watters?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I don't. I would have to read a milinfosum for every day of six months to answer the question. I don't think there is, and I have tried to find one and couldn't. But it is a clear memory of mine. Again, don't quote milinfosums as authority. You showed me one yesterday on the 25th of April, and on the first page was an absolute glaring mistake. The milinfosums represented, as I said yesterday, what we assessed at the time and often were only the judgement of a sergeant major or a very junior captain on what they had been told on debriefing patrols. They do not necessarily represent the facts or, indeed, the opinion of BritBat at the time. They were an internal document for internal use. We never expected, when we were producing them, that they would be held at a criminal tribunal as absolute fact. Some of it is absolute fact. Some of it is assessment, and some of that assessment, with hindsight, wasn't necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. But with no accusation intended or implication or innuendo, Colonel Watters, I think it would be fair to say that you have not seen any milinfosum that contains any reference to that incident that you have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need go over this. I mean if there are none, you can point it out to us in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to my final questions for you, Colonel Watters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we leave it, the witness has given evidence that Dario Kordic was involved in the release, as he understood it, of this convoy and said it had been done, it had been stopped, to make a point. Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it is in dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, let's try and finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think I will be able to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, you aren't aware of any information or facts that established Mr. Kordic played any role in the planning or execution of the military campaign in the Lasva Valley in April 1993, are you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: And equally I'm not aware he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, with respect to the subject of the evocative term "ethnic cleansing", that the Croats had also been victims of deliberate ethnic cleansing in the Lasva Valley, as well as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was no monopoly in Central Bosnia, in either the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, on ethnic cleansing or murder and dispossessing people of their houses and burning those houses. There was no monopoly on either of the three factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and it's your view that throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the time that you were there, those sorts of affairs were going on on both sides, or all three sides, really?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My final question for you is you were mentioned in Colonel Stewart's book. I would just like to read you a section from it and get your views on this particular observation, if I may. This is page 318 to 319. Colonel Stewart gives these views: "Bosnia is certainly complex beyond anyone's dreams. There are far more than three sides, Serb, Croat, and Muslim, what we hear about in the media. There are factions within groups and groups within factions, and without an established order, these different elements had created a situation as close to anarchy as I have yet witnessed. "Bosnia does not even recognise itself as a country. The main political parties and armies are all newly created. Even the differentiation between military and civilian is impossible. "Bosnia is undergoing a classic civil war fought by civilians against civilians, as a civilian one minute, as a soldier the next. "Bryan Watters, my second in command, remarked to me, when we were looking at an appalling atrocity, that there were few noble acts in a civil war." He also says: "A civilian soldier probably knows little about the established rules of war. The use of detainees for digging trenches in the front line, where they are liable to be shot by their own side, might make sense to him, but both the ICRC and we were incensed by it. 'It is strictly against the Geneva Convention,' we shout in exasperation. 'What's the Geneva Convention,' comes the reply. "How can someone like Commander Lucko in Turbe be expected to know all the details of the 'civilised' conduct of war? Less than two years ago, he was a teacher. He's had very little military training. What he is actually doing, of course, is defending his home or what is left of it." Did you and Colonel Watters [sic] discuss subjects such as that towards the end of your tour in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your question is obviously in error, because then I would be talking to myself. You mean Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did those reflect your views as well as his?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: To differing degrees. I always took a view that ignorance of the Geneva Convention and the chaos, confusion, and bitterness of a civil war gave nobody the authority to kill what I often described as the victims of Bosnia, those least able to defend themselves, and I don't think anyone had an excuse to do that, no matter what they were doing and what they were protecting. And so as I walked through fields of dead bodies, I didn't believe that the end had justified the means on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, I have one final question, since I have five minutes left. Do you remember discussing with Lieutenant Dooley what he did in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to be reminded, I'm afraid. I had lots of discussion with lots of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of Lieutenant Dooley telling you that he had picked up six bodies in Ahmici and then taken them to the cemetery that you have identified in the photograph, the aerial photograph, and dropped them off?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of discussing with him returning to Ahmici, picking up yet more bodies, about four or five, and then taking them to the cemetery and putting them in the same place?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you're saying that the bodies that I photographed early on the morning of the 16th were the bodies that BritBat had moved there, that is not possible because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Colonel Watters, I'm not making that suggestion at all.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right. I mean I don't have a memory of discussing that with Dooley. The only memory I have of discussing, in any detail, the movement of people and bodies was with a Colour-Sergeant Kicavinski (phoen), who had moved about 16 people in one of his Warriors, which was unusual. We were moving tens of dozens of bodies all over the place, and I don't, I'm afraid -- I apologise. I don't have a single recollection of a conversation with Dooley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you recall any reports that you received on the morning of the 16th of April that at least 17 civilian bodies had been picked up in Ahmici by your forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't give you the number, but I am aware that Colonel Stewart gave the order that we were to recover bodies, and our soldiers did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart gave that order?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was an order that Colonel Stewart had given before, that if we found bodies, we were to remove them from the scene of the fighting, and that was something that the soldiers did as a matter of course. We were -- usually we were removing wounded people, but with the wounded people, we also used to take bodies, and on occasion we would specifically mount a mission to remove bodies. I think I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, thank you very much for your testimony. I know it's been difficult. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, before you conclude, the passage which was alluded to before concerned British army doctrines, I think it was called --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: FIBUA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- of fighting in built-up areas, and the witness gave evidence about it. Now, the question here is, what is the relevance of this to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It seems to me, Your Honour, that there has been considerable discussion about the fighting that occurred in Ahmici, and it also seems to me that the military officers who had received extensive military training with the JNA, and who were presumably familiar with standard tactical doctrines such as those that prevailed in the British army, would employ those techniques in built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what is being suggested is that what happened in Ahmici was or may have been the result of the use of those sort of tactics; is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Although I will say, in light of the question that was posed to the Defence yesterday, the Defence's position is that we do not know specifically what happened in Ahmici; that's been the subject of a trial which has gone on for two and a half years and which is the subject of closing arguments as we speak. And our position is that our client had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I understand that. But at the same time, what happened in Ahmici is an issue in this case on which the Defence will put forward a case. Now, it may be that you say that you are not in a position to accept the evidence, but you're not in a position to dispute it. It will be helpful to the Trial Chamber to know what position you adopt. But meanwhile, the witness should have a chance to comment on the suggestion that what he saw in Ahmici may have been the result of the use of the sort of tactics he was describing. Can you comment on that, Colonel, or not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only comment, sir, on what I saw afterwards. And the systematic destruction of every Muslim house in Ahmici would not, in my experience, have been what I would expect to see after a FIBUA assault of the type described by the Defence counsel, in line with British doctrine, which he asked me to agree with. It was far too systematic and didn't -- I mean, there weren't the marks on the walls of suppressive fire; there weren't signs of mortar and artillery; and the sniper positions that we identified around the village, which I took around and pointed out to the U.N. investigators, were more doctrinally in line with other procedures that we would use to secure an area and try and capture the people in it, having put out stops to prevent likely enemy escaping. Also within our doctrine is the opportunity, (a), for civilians and noncombatants to be removed from any area to be assaulted by a high-intensity assault, and also the opportunity for people to surrender and be taken as prisoners of war rather than to be killed. And there was nothing in what I visited in Ahmici that led me to believe that that assault had been conducted within any rules of war or the Geneva Convention. It looked to me, as I said yesterday, as a massacre and a systematic destruction of animals, people, and houses in a specific village, similar to things I've seen in other parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to ask any question, Mr. Sayers, arising from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It seems to me that that is your opinion, Colonel Watters, but wouldn't you concede that there would be room for disagreement between professionals in your area regarding that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would be happy to debate with other professionals their view based on their experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can look forward to your defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions, unless the Trial Chamber has any for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there's going to be a break, can I simply ask that the witness is allowed to look at unmarked but tagged copies of the two passages of transcript in respect to which he said they ought to be seen in context? It will save time for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Watters. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I am a lawyer from Rijeka, and with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, we are the Defence counsel of the second accused in this case, Mr. Mario Cerkez. I do not speak the same language as you, so you know what the method is: We have to have a pause between the question and the answer, because of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to that part of your testimony of yesterday in which you mentioned your contact with the commander of the Vitez Brigade, and that was on page 35, line 16. You said that you had talked to the commander of the brigade. You mentioned his last name, which probably because of the record -- because of language difficulties was hard to record. You could not recall the first name, so let us clarify this. Were you referring to Mr. Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I remember Mr. Cerkez's Christian name is Mario now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your knowledge of the chain of command of the HVO led you to know that he was the commander of an HVO brigade based in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that after that, and we are referring to the morning of the 16th, you went to the commander on the Muslim side in Vitez. What was his name? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'd have to look at my notes. You mentioned language earlier; I'm afraid those names do not stay in my memory very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Sefkija Sivro (sic), if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that the person who took part later on in the negotiations -- excuse me; I apologise: Sefkija Dzidic. I made a mistake. I made a mistake. Was it the same person who on that day and the following day came to your offices in Bila to participate in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I remember, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to introduce a document for the witness to look at, so would the usher please take the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D36/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Watters, the document I have shown to you is a report by Colonel Blaskic to his main staff in Mostar reporting about this meeting which took place on the 16th in Bila, and the HVO representatives listed here are Marko Prskalo and Zoran Pilicic, and you mentioned these yesterday. Would you agree, because lower down, the representatives of the Republic of B and H, the army of the Republic of B and H, are listed as Sefkija Dzidic and Sifet Sivro, do you agree that the above-mentioned Prskalo and Pilicic, as members of the command of the Operative Zone of which Blaskic was the commander, represented him?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: My understanding of the meeting at 12.30 in Bila School was I was talking to representatives of the opposing factions in Vitez, and at that time a scale of the fighting was not yet clear in our mind, and I was dealing solely with the fighting in and around Vitez. I understood I was talking to representatives of the two brigades or the two commanders within Vitez. As I see, my own name is incorrect in this document. I'm not sure what else might be correct or incorrect. Does that answer your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Partly, yes.
