But from what you said, it is evident that on the 16th, in the morning, as you said, you immediately asked to contact the commander of the Operative Zone, Blaskic, and you obviously agreed to his sending representatives to the meeting. After that, you looked for Mario Cerkez. It is not quite clear from your response whether you actually met him or not, but it seems that some kind of contact was established which was sufficient, and he agreed to come to the meeting. Do we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember seeing Mr. Cerkez in his headquarters in the cinema building in Vitez on that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But up to 12.30 hours, or a little before that when your people took their representatives into their vehicle, were these negotiations taken over at a higher level because their representatives arrived at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The imperative of that meeting was to stop the fighting in Vitez, and I was willing to risk the lives of my officers and soldiers to collect any representatives to come to a meeting to stop the fighting. My perception at the meeting was that those people represented those forces fighting in Vitez, and I conducted negotiations to try and stop that fighting. Those negotiations failed, because the fighting did not stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Watters, from what you said, it is clear that you had some basic information about the chain of command. Was Colonel Blaskic Cerkez's superior, since he was in command of one of the HVO brigades?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was our understanding and my understanding, that Mr. Cerkez was a subordinate commander to Colonel Blaskic. Mario Cerkez commanded the Vitez Brigade, and Colonel Tihomir Blaskic was the regional commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If I can draw your attention to Mr. Sefkija Djidic, whom we have just mentioned and who was also mentioned in the Blaskic case, on page 1209, when referring to this meeting and in answer to the question concerning the meeting of the 16th of April and the agreement on a ceasefire, he responded the following. I will read it in English, because I have the original English transcript, so it will speed things up. So he said the following. I quote: (In English) " [Previous interpretation continues]... of the British Battalion managed to organise a meeting which was attended on the part of the HVO by an officer called Zoran Pilicic. He was a staff officer in the Operative Zone. I think he stood in for Mr. Blaskic, and another officer called Marko Prskalo [no interpretation]... the wish of the British Battalion was to achieve an immediate ceasefire." (Interpretation) So do you agree that this is the meeting referred to?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Sefkija Djidic, as the local commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was more familiar with the personnel and the level of command they had?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sefkija Djidic referred to the same meeting in his statement made to the investigators on the 17th and 24th of July, 1995, and we received this statement from the Prosecution. On page 10, if I may read from the statement, he says the following: (In English) "The joint meeting was organised where peace was attempted, but it was not successful. Lieutenant Colonel Stewart from BritBat was the mediator. The main topic was a suggestion by the HVO for the surrender of Stari Vitez and Gacice and Veceriska. The HVO said that if this was not done, those villages would be destroyed." (Interpretation) He says: (In English) "The negotiations continued for three days. At this meeting, neither Blaskic or Cerkez were present." (Interpretation) So do you agree that at the meeting, it was obviously representatives and not the direct commanders of the HVO who took part at the talks?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, there is some confusion. There were several meetings that day. The meeting I'm referring to, which I think was the meeting you showed me in the previous document, I chaired, and it was the first meeting at about 12.00 or so. Colonel Stewart returned from Zenica later in the day and chaired more meetings, and so I think that this evidence is talking about a later meeting that Colonel Stewart chaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But we agree that there were at least two or three meetings on three consecutive days?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At least, yes. Do we agree that at least on the first two days, Cerkez did not participate in the meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I certainly had a meeting with him, as we referred to earlier. Whether Mr. Cerkez attended the meetings personally, I don't remember, and as the military commander who was fighting with his soldiers, I would be surprised if he was able to attend those meetings. But I have a vivid memory of a meeting with him and the BiH commander, in which we discussed a range of topics including, I think, the fact that Mr. Cerkez's family actually lived in Kruscica that his forces were attacking, and I remember saying that this was a very screwed-up place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In any case, from what you have said so far, you drew a distinction both as regards the location and the level of command between the command of the Operative Zone, which was based at the hotel, where the commander was Blaskic, and the command of the Vitez Brigade, which was based in the cinema building or the open university building, as they called it, where Cerkez was the commander; there is no doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No doubt at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the morning of the 16th, you attempted to establish contact and to organise a meeting for peace talks; we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You achieved this, to a certain extent, because the first meeting was held at around noon on your premises and was attended by representatives of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding that the only thing that you are not certain of is whether the persons mentioned, Prskalo and Pilicic, were representing the brigade or the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: To be honest, sir, I didn't give it any thought, as the esoterics of where they came from within the HVO wasn't my concern, as long as they represented those people who could stop the fighting. I have no further comment to make about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go on to another topic. I would like to ask the usher to take out document D24/1. You have already seen this document. I would like to draw your attention to the signatures on the second page. As far as I can understand, you later learned -- I apologise. As far as I was able to understand, you later learned that this ceasefire had been agreed on.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Isn't it confusing, or how did you explain the fact that between the 16th and the 18th, you were attempting to persuade the representatives of the local forces of both of the sides involved in the conflict to sign a ceasefire or to withdraw, and only four days later, at the top level, their commanders in chief, Petkovic and Halilovic, signed an agreement that in paragraph 1 it is evident that they were members of the same army; how did you explain this to yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would probably explain it by drawing your attention to the document from Colonel Blaskic in which he described the BiH forces in Vitez, in that document you've just shown me, as the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is all confusing and contradictory?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was our welcome to Bosnia, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, you mentioned on page 15 the checkpoint on the road where there was soldiers in black uniforms who belonged to the Croatian side and who seemed to belong to a kind of special purpose unit and who made problems about the passage of the convoy, and in spite of Blaskic's authorisation for the convoy to pass through, they said they did not get their orders from Blaskic and refused to let it pass. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One of your aims, as you explained, was to find out what the chain of command was, what the relations were, to get to know who the commanders were and where they were so that you could communicate with the local forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know which units, at least in the area of Central Bosnia, or maybe only in Vitez, what forces made up the HVO under the command of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I had a detailed understanding as far as we knew it, and it was put into our milinfosums and situation reports. I can't actually today recite the names of the different operational zones, the brigades they all contained, and who their commanders were. I don't retain that sort of information in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the Witness D27/2. Could you place it on the ELMO, sir? Or if you need time, please take it. (Interpretation) I apologise for the fact that the copy is not very good, but we have seen worse. However, this is part of the supporting material we were given, and we do not have a better copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document was drawn up by UNPROFOR, as is stated on it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean, I don't remember the specific document, but it says "U.N., Restricted." It looks like the sort of document we used to produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this diagram shows that in the Central Bosnia Operative Group, which is the little box at the top, that from the part we see on the left, there is the Vitez Brigade commanded by Mario Cerkez; the next little box to the right is the Frankopan Brigade, and it is -- the name is not quite legible, but it's obviously based in another area; and then there are the two at the end, the Vitezovi, SPF, special forces, probably; and to the right, the military police, which seems to be based in Vitez and commanded by Ljubicic. Do you agree that we can conclude from this that in the operational zone, there were at least four units, and the Frankopan Brigade seems not to have been based in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is part of a document. It would show other operational zones that came under the regional command, but as you say, that would appear to be that the Frankopan Brigade was not the Vitez Brigade; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you. Frankopan is one brigade and Vitez is another brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the two to the very right are not brigades, but some other kind of units?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that they all evidently fall under the command of Blaskic's operational zone?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: You'll see a question mark above the "Special Forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, with a certain reserve, if there is a question mark there.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We would have to explain our understanding of the use of special forces, who can be grouped under a brigade or region, but who also will have additional chains of command, which is why they're called "special." So I don't want to state in evidence that because this picture shows them underneath on a wiring diagram, that that is the chain of command in which they operate. They would operate additional chains of command, which is why they would be designated as special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. But can they be under the command, in this case, of the brigades which are in the same line of hierarchy, at least in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But this is not evident from this diagram?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's why I said you cannot treat this diagram as doctrine. It is merely a way of trying to express to ourselves particular groupings. Those special forces units could operate from the very highest levels, directed by central government, or they could operate subordinate to a battalion or brigade commander. It would all depend on their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, you said that in Vitez you recognised some units. Which units did you recognise as separate units forming part of the HVO? Which of them can you enumerate today? Evidently the brigade was there, because we have been talking about it; but in practice, during the time you were in Vitez, did you see any other HVO units who were active there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was another HVO unit that was based in what we called the Bungalow, which dressed differently, held itself apart from the Vitez Brigade unit, and appeared to operate sometimes on similar tasks and sometimes on different tasks. They wore different uniforms and tended to carry different weapons on different days. We didn't consider them to be part of, routinely, the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us if you managed to become more familiar with the chain of command in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't say "better"; I would say we grappled all the time to remain familiar with the two chains of command and their dispositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in the area of the Lasva Valley, there were also active parts of the 3rd Corps, based in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the 7th Muslim Brigade was also active there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade operated or was alleged to operate throughout Central Bosnia, and yes, we had reports of the 7th Muslim Brigade operating south of Zenica, down towards Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the 314th Mountain Brigade operated there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Today, sir, I can't remember. But if you say that it was in our milinfosums, at the time, we believed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. And do you still remember the name of any of the Muslim commanders of the time in the area?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: We've mentioned the commander in Vitez, and I mostly dealt at 3rd Corps with Enver Hadzihasanovic and his deputy, Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does the name ^ "Dzananovic" ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not today, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 325th?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, sir. Our liaison officers may well have known him. I don't recollect having any personal relationship with him. I may well have met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And Merdan, again, in relation to the 325th, would that mean anything to you? Does it say anything?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Merdan was the deputy commander of 3rd Corps, so by definition would have been the deputy commander, and at times, in the absence of his commander, he would have commanded those units of the 3rd Corps. If there was another man called Merdan, I haven't met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, right. This is the man I meant, and I also meant the 325th, yes. Let us move on to some other subjects. Some place in the beginning of your testimony here, I believe it was page 12, you spoke about a strong offensive of Serb forces from the direction of Banja Luka; that is, from the north-northwest, southward. As a matter of fact, you said they were headed for Gornji Vakuf, and that they were stopped somewhere near Turbe or Novi Travnik. Do you remember the context? Do you remember what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said they were heading for Travnik, not Gornji Vakuf, and they stopped at Turbe, having captured Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you know, why did they stop, or how were they stopped? Did they do it themselves at Turbe, or rather on Vlasic, near Turbe, to the north-northwest of Travnik, or they simply could not move forward because of defence forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our judgement at the time was if they had wanted to, they could have swept completely through. There wasn't sufficient resistance to stop them. They decided to stop. The reasons they decided to stop, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. And that weak resistance that was offered, did you know at the time that individual sectors north-northwest of Novi Travnik, or rather above Turbe, on Vlasic, were held both by the HVO and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware that they were holding sectors along Vlasic and around through to Turbe. Our assessment at the time, and that of Colonel Stewart, was that the Serbs had the capability to push through, and we had made contingency plans as to what we were going to do if the Serbs actually overran Vitez and the base we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So although both the ABiH and the HVO held certain sectors on Vlasic, they would nevertheless have not been able to prevent the onslaught of the Serb forces had they been bent to move on? They wouldn't have been able to stop them?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know something about something that happened before you arrived, but perhaps during your briefings you might have learned something about that, and that is that sometime in late 1992, in November, the HVO forces on that Vlasic line, they were joined by some forces from Herzegovina as a reinforcement on that defence line, and there were names, ^ Anto Prkic and ^ Dzanana were mentioned in that regard. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not in detail, no, sir. My background reading was just that, to establish the situation. I was more concerned with the present than the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree -- of course, if you can remember -- whether the Brigade Stjepan Tomasevic was based in Novi Travnik and was active in the area, an HVO brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific names of the brigades there. I am clear that the line in Turbe was held by joint forces of the BiH and HVO, who would continuously argue over the proportion of their soldiers who were in the line. It wasn't a very easy alliance. I was also aware of other areas, specifically Maglaj, where there was a joint BiH/HVO brigade, and that brigade, in my view, was the only one that actually was cohesive as a joint brigade. The remainder were fractioned between BiH and HVO and weren't properly integrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to round off these operations against the Serbs, would you -- do you know if on the very day when the conflict broke out in Vitez -- that is, on the 16th of April, 1993 -- both armies were still on the defence lines with some forces? I mean on that defence line on Vlasic above Turbe. Did you have any knowledge and information about that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have a memory of visiting Turbe and being told that the HVO forces had largely left the line and the BiH forces were more or less on their own there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were told this by representatives of the army of B and H?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was told it by the commander in Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who belonged to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity of checking, of seeing with your own eyes, if the HVO was still there in that sector which they used to hold before?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that visit, I couldn't see any HVO soldiers, and within the command group, I didn't see any represented, which in the past, they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That visit was when?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly which day. It was prior to the 15th of April. It was in April. It might even have been quite early in April. I would probably have to go back and check our logs to see when I went to Turbe, on which day, if that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another area. You mentioned that on the 15th, HVO commander Zivko Totic was abducted, and that his escort in the vehicle had been killed, and that you thought that it might be the turning point in the relations. But do you remember that three days before that in Novi Travnik, four officers of the HVO had been abducted and it also led to mounting tension?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that's the incident where they were going to move at night down the road from Novi Travnik to Gornji Vakuf. If that's the incident, yes, I do remember that, and they were abducted, and that certainly raised tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I believe we shall agree that in that former half of April, there were a whole series of incidents, bigger or smaller, and the ones we just mentioned were simply more significant and that it rendered the whole situation much more complex. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information in relation to attempts to trace Zivko Totic and those HVO who had been abducted? Have you heard of some contacts and even cooperation between army BH units and HVO units in Novi Travnik itself, and that, in a manner of speaking, your men also tried to help, rather mediated in those attempts to try to trace those men?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Colonel Stewart did it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear if local commanders in Novi Travnik, that is, Sabljic, who commanded the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik, and Bislim Zurapi, who commanded the 8th Brigade, had also agreed to and even maintained joint roadblocks on all the entrances and exits from Novi Travnik precisely because of those abductions?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was an initial proposal for joint checkpoints. I don't think they lasted very long, and there was no doubt in our minds that the hierarchy of the BiH appeared to be angry at these abductions and did not appear to have orchestrated them. But as I've said, when dealing with all sides in Bosnia, and you alluded to it yourself earlier, things were not always what they seemed, and we remained or we tried always to maintain an open mind on everything that we observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, right, but wouldn't you agree that that road, in view of all those checkpoints, that it was the road to Vitez which was kept under control?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I've said, I mean all roads around Central Bosnia were patrolled and there were checkpoints on them, and the checkpoints tended to be manned by the soldier -- were always manned, with one or two exceptions where there were joint checkpoints, were always manned by the forces that actually either were the ethnic majority in the area or physically controlled the area in terms of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us then move on to another matter. It has to do with Novi Travnik. You mentioned that the conflict in Novi Travnik also began on the 16th of April, and I should say it was quite clear, from a number of documents, that there were three conflicts in Novi Travnik; one in June '92 -- as early as June '92. It burst out and then calmed down. Then in December '92. I believe you know about that. The third conflict in Novi Travnik occurred only in June; that is, the 9th of June, 1993. In Novi Travnik, there were no conflicts that would be simultaneous with the conflicts in Vitez. Was that simply a slip of the tongue or is it that you hold a different opinion as to that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was conflict in and around our location in Bila School, which we used to describe as being in Novi Travnik or close to Novi Travnik, and there was fighting on the night of the 16th, 17th, 18th between HV and BiH all around the area of our school and we ourselves were fired on and mortared repeatedly, and that was why I described fighting being in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Geographically speaking, Bila, where you were based, is in the Lasva Valley, and not far from it is where the road to Novi Travnik forks off, isn't that correct, and there are about 15 kilometres to Novi Travnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to look on a map. I mean I don't think Bila, as a name, was on our maps, the nearest sort of town to where we were. Halfway between Novi Travnik and Vitez, sometimes we would describe ourselves as in Vitez; other times we would describe ourselves in Novi Travnik. The actual fighting I don't think was centred on Novi Travnik. It was in the village down the road from Novi Travnik, shortly down the road towards Gornji Vakuf. I can't remember the name of the village. I wouldn't specifically say and have no recollection of specific fighting in the middle of Novi Travnik. As I say, it's an esoteric argument. We considered ourselves sort of halfway between Vitez and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. I believe we've clarified it. Thank you. Let us move on to another area. You spoke about artillery weapons, large calibre. I believe you said 155 millimetres, relating to the shelling of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of that sort of calibre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you said that those weapons were around Mosunj; that is, not far from the place where your base was located. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was one particular piece not far away that we heard regularly firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who commanded those artillery pieces; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did know the names of the individual officers who commanded the individual pieces. The actual artillery would be controlled, in our view and on our information, at regional level. Whether the regional commander would chart the authority or support of those particular mortars and artillery pieces to individual brigade commanders would be a matter for the regional commander. We wouldn't necessarily know the detail of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: By "the regional level", you mean the Operative Zone in our particular case?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Operational Zone, the regional commander or the brigade commander. Those assets would probably be commanded or come under the overall command of the regional commander. Who he would delegate authority to have support for those artillery pieces would be his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) May I ask the usher, please, to assist me to show D60/1, to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to paragraph 3 on page 2, so it's the paragraph in the middle of the page. It refers to those artillery pieces that you just mentioned, but it also says that the commander of that particular unit told you that the army of B and H was launching an offensive north of Kula and that that was their operational target, and that he also told you, and that is the last sentence, that, "I had never conducted any operations in the direction of Zenica," and that their role, their operations, were purely defensive. I presume this was the kind of information which was then put in the milinfosum by your people, by your men, just as they heard it. Would that be correct to assume?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. What that is simply a recording of what was said to some of our soldiers by a particular HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, as we already said, it may but need not be true, but somebody must have told it to your people; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To conclude, I should like to ask one more question. You spoke about it and also showed us on the map, all the main roads in that particular area, and you said that to the west, Vitez and Busovaca, and that all the main roads to those towns were cut off or, rather, that the Croat community there was cut off and, to all intents and purposes, isolated. My learned friend for the Prosecution asked you then if one could say that on the 18th and 19th and the 20th of April, the Muslim counteroffensive proved very successful, and you agreed with that. You said that it had been very successful. I do not want to dispute that. All I want to ask you is to confirm, if you can, or, rather, to say whether it would be fair to conclude from that that any kind of supply that is at the very survival of the population in that besieged area, in that surrounded area of Vitez and Busovaca, had been cut off and that it really -- that their life depended on the goodwill of the Muslim side, which held all the access roads to the area, would that be true, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Watters. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two passages of transcript put to you by Mr. Sayers. Have you now looked at them in their context?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The question I was actually asked was, "Did the ICRC, the International Committee for the Red Cross, hand information over to the HVO?" And the answer I gave was, "No. They wouldn't give information to us either."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second passage, the passage dealing with knowledge of Blaskic providing names or sending names up his chain of command, did you read that in its context overall?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's the actual context of that passage?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: The actual context is the fact that although Colonel Blaskic may or may not have passed names of those that he had been told or, indeed, himself knew had conducted the massacre in Ahmici, he took no direct action against those soldiers, which I believed and my colleagues believed was a total dereliction of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You also make plain, at page 3461, that what you were speaking about was information that had come to you about Colonel Stewart handing or supplying the names in whatever way he did to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same as you've explained to this Tribunal today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up on just a few of the points that you have been asked about, the convoy in Mostar, was any other name identified, apart from Kordic's, as a person able to release that convoy?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, sir, and we specifically -- I specifically asked headquarters, U.N. in Kiseljak, to speak to Mostar, to General Petkovic, to ask him to specifically order Mr. Kordic to release that convoy before I ordered an assault on Busovaca to take it back by force of arms, which was raising the stakes so far as we had not at that point directly attacked the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blaskic saying that it was the Serbs who had attacked Ahmici or may have done, did he give, in your presence or to your knowledge, any other possible explanation?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: When he was told that that was blatantly ridiculous, he also then said that the Muslims had done it themselves. I can't remember the exact words, but it was something along those lines. Essentially, everybody but the HVO had conducted the massacre in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Questions this morning about fighting in a built-up area and your comments on that, just these additional points.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I can just add something to that, I was trying to put in context why it did not conform with a FIBUA attack on a defended locality, and the most stark reason that presented itself was the absolute lack of damage to the Croat houses that abutted the bottom of the Muslim area of Ahmici, and the doctrine for assaulting an armed locality or defended locality could not possibly have been so surgical in destroying certain houses and leaving others totally unscathed. It was just beyond comprehension.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was one of the points I was going to raise. Under this so-called doctrine, once a house is taken, is it necessary to burn it and destroy it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: You certainly wouldn't do that, because you would use it yourself as a defended locality, which would be the purpose of you capturing the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If, in taking any such house, there were occupants, civilian or otherwise, would it be appropriate to kill them?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean, it would be a contravention of the Geneva Convention, and a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been suggested to you that there might be expert opinion to the contrary effect. First, have you at any time heard, seen, read, any expert opinion to the effect that this was mere evidence of performance of fighting in a built-up area?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was put to me during the last trial that that's what it was, and I refuted it. As I said earlier, I would debate with anyone of military experience who would put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you in fact ever had the chance to see anybody's expert report or to hear any expert witness advancing this theory?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No one has ever done it in my hearing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If anybody were to provide you with an expert report that they may hold, would you be prepared to assist us with your comments on it?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Zenica, the inaccuracy or limited accuracy of artillery at distance: You acknowledge that. Is that something that must, of necessity, be generally known?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say of the legitimacy of attacking with such imprecision a town where there may be a military base?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've been to that military base. It's located in a factory complex in the town. Without giving a very detailed explanation of how you coordinate and direct artillery fire, in my professional judgement, it would be impossible to engage that building with artillery fire, specifically, knowing the dispositions of the HVO and the BiH. The HVO would have to be able to have eyes on that building to direct the fire into it, and the risk of correcting the initial fire onto a specific building in a civilian city is not an act of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your opinion about Zenica, and its similarity to the truck bomb and its characterisation, displaced in any way by the proposition relating to the military headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about accusations of attacks on Croats, and I think there was one passage in the summary that I overlooked dealing with, but which arises in connection with that. It's paragraph 29. On the 24th of April, was there an allegation of massacres committed by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were allegations of massacres committed by Muslims, and each one of those we investigated to the very best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, villages of Grahovici and Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I personally went to those two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find any evidence of massacres?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I think we found two bodies in Grahovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose ethnicity you assumed or calculated to be what?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I -- I assumed that they were Croat. They were two -- they were two old men who were lying dead in a field, without shoes on. It looked like they had been either running away and shot or told to run away and shot. I took them to be Croats. Because I'd been asked to go and investigate it by the Croats, I made that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The legitimate --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, I also investigated an allegation, personally, of a massacre in Jelinak, which is just above the Kaonik junction out of Busovaca, which was a Croat town, and there was the -- there was the scene of fighting, and buildings had been damaged, and there was one partly-burnt body of a man, and that was the only evidence we found. But the buildings had not been destroyed in the way that they had been in Ahmici, but they had bullet strike marks on them, RPG-7 rocket marks on them, but they had not been destroyed. And we did not find the evidence of any bodies other than one man -- which is still one too many, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You distinguished between combat power and manpower. Are you able to express a view, or the view held at the time, as to the comparative combat power of these two forces?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The point I was making there was I didn't want the Court to draw from the fact that in manpower terms, the 3-to-1 approximate sort of differential would mean that the Muslim forces actually had three times the capability. They were less well-armed. They didn't have the quantities of heavy weapons. They didn't have the quantity of the anti-aircraft weapons, that you saw yesterday, mounted on flatbeds, which were very powerful weapons indeed. A great many of these people we saw had shotguns and sort of farmer's-type weapons. Now, within the BiH, there were equally professional units as existed in the HVO, but they also had sort of vast numbers, if you like, of poorly armed infantry. One of the differences which possibly accounted for the success of their counterattack was a greater willingness on the part of the BiH to mount infantry assaults, which didn't seem to be a favoured option of the HVO, and possibly because the BiH had more infantry and more numbers. But the actual combat power and capability of those large numbers of infantry was extremely limited, due to their lack of mortar, artillery, and automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The objective of controlling supply routes you accepted as a legitimate objective; does that affect, one way or another, your opinion on the legitimacy of attacking the villages in the way that we've heard about?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. What I said was the defence and the control of arterial routes was a strategic objective to secure the political cohesiveness and survival of those Croat communities. I also said that the end state didn't justify the means, and the ethnic cleansing that I personally witnessed, and the wholesale destruction of villages, and the murder of the people in those villages to secure the routes, certainly wasn't justified at all. The military operations should be looked at separately from the requirement to remove people of different cultural or ethnic groups from your specific area, and I think I tried to explain that in the context of the double objectives with the establishment or the potential establishment of the Vance-Owen Plan, which we saw both within the Serb- and the Croat-dominated areas, of removing the ethnic minorities to establish a firmer control. I'm sorry, I haven't answered that particularly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have three more questions, I think, Your Honour, all of which will be short, or may be short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first form the view that you held about the existence of a dual chain of command?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Personally, after the incident with the convoy and the -- outside Busovaca, which Mr. Kordic had abducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did other evidence at the time fit with or contradict that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was quite clear that it existed. My first personal evidence that it existed, and at times contradicted itself, was that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You made reference to the letter to your father and a sentence being taken out of context. Is there anything more you want to add to that? I'm not sure that we dealt with it in that way yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was quite surprised to see that letter. I was -- I mean, I was writing a letter to my father, who had fought in the Second World War, to try to explain to him what we were doing. And I was slightly surprised, having been told that the Defence counsel and I spoke the same language, that he didn't understand the first sentence. I hadn't written to my father since I had been in Bosnia, and that was playing heavily on my conscience, so I wrote to him. The letter, which I wrote quite late at night, gained a little more momentum that I originally intended it to, and if it was read by the Defence counsel, then he would understand what I meant by the movement of forces. I would also just like to explain -- which I don't think I really did properly -- the movement of those injured people from just south of Vitez, from Kruscica, on the night of the 16th. We went into the village of Kruscica, which was under attack by Croat forces, by ground forces, artillery, and mortars. As a precursor to the ceasefire agreements of the 16th, the BiH had told us that because the HVO had cut the road from Kruscica to Vitez, they were unable to treat their casualties in the medical centre which their doctors were stationed in Vitez. They also had heard rumours that their doctors had been killed. I later went to that medical centre, and there were two dead men wearing doctor's clothes in that medical centre. That night, when I arrived in the village, my soldiers and myself were actually quite frightened, because it was a very dangerous place. We had already had two of our soldiers killed earlier -- or one killed and the other one who killed himself because he couldn't face what he was doing -- and I was very angry when I went in the cellar and found that I had been lied to by the BiH forces, and that that there were men wounded in the cellar, and not women. They were in civilian clothes, and they had lumps out of their bodies and were bleeding to death. I had to make a decision, whether I left them to die or I put them in our ambulances and took them to the hospital. I believed that, in all consciousness, I could not leave them to die, even though they weren't the people I had been told about. So we put them in our ambulances. I registered my anger at being lied to with the BiH commander and returned to Vitez and took them to hospital in Travnik. I then reported to Colonel Blaskic personally what had happened, because the Croat authorities had given their permission for us to go and get these wounded civilians. And having recorded with him what I'd done, undertook to do something of equal consequence for Colonel Blaskic on a future occasion, should he require it, which he did later, and we moved a comparable number of wounded Croat soldiers from Vitez to their hospital in Novi Travnik. And so I would just like to make sure the record is straight that at no time did we ever move armed Muslim or Croat soldiers within our protection, other than with the agreement of their own commanders, to facilitate our mission statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question. One document that I can help everyone with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked questions about the firepower of the Warriors, and also I think their presence in the area of Ahmici early on the relevant morning. What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS (Resumed)
utterances.text: Their purpose was actually to reconnoitre the scenes of fighting, and they used the considerable protection they have to be able to move into areas of fighting, taking quite a lot of direct hits themselves, and they were used on the initiative of the individual vehicle commanders and platoon commanders to move civilians caught up in the fighting to places of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice that the document D27/2, the wire diagram that the witness was asked about, does not have the footnotes clearly on it. I've managed to find a better version. I can distribute that straight away. I don't think any issue will arise from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It can be distributed on Monday morning. We're going to adjourn now. Colonel, thank you very much for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until Monday morning, half past 9.00. Court III again; we will try and sit there.
